cards.back: A **reaction mechanism** is a proposed sequence of elementary steps showing a possible route from reactants to products. It is more than the starting and ending substances.

cards.front: How do you get the overall reaction from a mechanism's steps?
cards.back: **Add** all the steps, then **cancel** equal amounts of substances that appear on both sides. The remaining equation is the overall reaction.
cards.hint: Cancel only equal amounts of the same substance.

cards.front: How can you tell an intermediate from a catalyst?
cards.back: An **intermediate** is formed before it is consumed. A **catalyst** is consumed before it is regenerated. Both cancel from the overall equation.
cards.hint: Look at which event happens first.

cards.front: What is the net equation for $\mathrm{NO_2+NO_2\rightarrow NO_3+NO}$ followed by $\mathrm{NO_3+CO\rightarrow NO_2+CO_2}$?
cards.back: $\mathrm{NO_2+CO\rightarrow NO+CO_2}$. Adding the steps and canceling one $\mathrm{NO_3}$ and one $\mathrm{NO_2}$ gives this.
cards.hint: Write out every substance on each side before canceling.

cards.back: An **intermediate** is produced in one mechanism step and consumed in a later step. It therefore cancels when the steps are added.

cards.front: Is every substance that cancels out of the steps an intermediate?
cards.back: No. A substance consumed first and regenerated later is a **catalyst**, not an intermediate.
cards.hint: Check the order in which the substance appears.

cards.front: Steps $\mathrm{A+C\rightarrow AC}$ and $\mathrm{AC+B\rightarrow AB+C}$ give what overall equation?
cards.back: $\mathrm{A+B\rightarrow AB}$. C is a catalyst and AC is an intermediate, so neither appears in the net equation.
cards.hint: Cancel C and AC after adding the steps.

cards.front: What does one elementary step represent?
cards.back: One **molecular event** within the reaction mechanism.

cards.front: Why is CO a reactant, not an intermediate, in the NO2 example?
cards.back: CO enters in the second step and becomes part of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ without being regenerated. So it stays on the reactant side of the net equation.
cards.hint: Ask whether the substance is regenerated later.

cards.front: Why can the overall reaction alone not establish a unique mechanism?
cards.back: It shows only the **net change**. Different sequences of steps can produce the same net change.
cards.hint: Think about what cancels when steps are added.

cards.back: A **regenerated substance** is consumed in one mechanism step and produced again in a later step.
A **net equation** shows the reactants consumed and products formed after matching substances cancel. It leaves out substances that were produced and later consumed.
